cues.txt: [HOST] Hello everyone, and welcome back for our
lunchtime conversation.
So this conversation is with Daniel Lurie,
who is the mayor of San Francisco.
Daniel was born and raised in San Francisco.
He majored in political science at Duke University and earned a
master's in public policy from UC Berkeley's Goldman School.
In 2005, shortly after he finished his master's
degree, he founded and led Tipping Point Community,
a pioneer in anti-poverty initiatives across the Bay Area.
He also led the Bid Committee and the Host
Committee for Super Bowl 50.
Please join me in welcoming Mayor Lurie.
(applause)
[DANIEL LURIE] Let's go.
Oh, boy.
Oh, I know too many people in this room.
[HOST] Okay, well, we'll just open up to Q&A to start off.
[AUDIENCE MEMBER] Seriously.
[HOST] How you doing?
So I'm really happy to have you here.
We're both political scientists by training as undergraduates.
I'm also happy to have you here.
[DANIEL LURIE] I took a few classes in political science.
You are the real deal.
[HOST] You discovered there's something useful to do with your life.
So, but also I grew up a bit like you,
I grew up in the Bay Area.
I love San Francisco, lived there for a while in the 1990s.
Although I think living in San Francisco for a Stanford
alum is far from unique.
From what I hear, there's like 10,000
Stanford alumni living in the city of San Francisco.
So I guess I'm not particularly special in
having done that at some point.
But I want to jump in and
talk about sort of-
The policy initiatives and what you're doing in San Francisco.
So a big part of your plan for San Francisco
includes improving public safety, reducing disorder,
addressing homelessness, the drug crisis,
and those are challenging things.
They're a big deal for the residents of the city.
They're a big deal for the city's image.
And frankly, they come with a lot
of stereotypes too, because a lot of people
think of those as being super intractable problems.
[AUDIENCE MEMBER] Mm-hmm.
[HOST] Either just in terms of getting people the help or
the policies that they need, and sometimes people think San
Francisco can't do the things that would be needed to be done.
Yeah.
It's a famously liberal city, and a lot of people sort of
don't think San Francisco's up for, up to the task.
Yep. So I'm curious how you're approaching this.
[DANIEL LURIE] Well, I think first off, I would say, first,
thank you for having me.
It's an honor to be with all of you.
You know, we talk a lot
about our progressive values in San Francisco.
And we have, and we have them, and I lean into those.
But frankly, there's nothing progressive-
About driving by or walking by somebody
that is passed out on the sidewalk.
Someone actually just brought up Fillmore Street,
and I used to live right off of Fillmore Street.
And this morning I was driving down Fillmore Street.
And my team, the detail, the police officer,
we saw somebody asleep on the concrete at 8:00 this morning,
and we got out of the car and we checked on the person.
There is nothing progressive about allowing somebody
to sleep on the street and not able to do well.
So we're focused on common sense solutions, getting
people off the street and into treatment beds, recovery beds.
We stood up 600 treatment beds last year in San Francisco.
I made a promise on the campaign trail that we would
stand up 1,500 shelter beds.
And then I've said this a couple times,
when people are like, "Don't—"
Don't talk about what you didn't follow through on,
but I like to talk about what the campaign was 1,500 beds.
And then I got in the office and my team,
we realized standing up 1,500
just normal shelter beds is not appropriate.
Getting someone that is addicted to fentanyl
into a shelter is not going to help that person.
So we want to stand up the right kind of beds,
and the right kind of beds are recovery and treatment beds.
So we have not done the 1,500 shelter beds, but we did do 600
recovery and treatment beds.
So everyone in San Francisco believes in
taking care of people.
And what we were doing as a city
was not taking care of people.
We were letting people use on the street, die on our streets.
Three years ago, we had
850-some-odd people die of
overdose in San Francisco.
The last two years that's come down, but last year was still
over 620.
We're heading in the right direction,
but there is nothing okay about those numbers.
So, and I think everybody,
the vast majority of San Franciscans believe that.
Now, on the public safety front
We have made real strides.
Crime last year was down 30% citywide.
It was down 40% in our downtown corridor.
And those numbers actually continue to go further down
in this first quarter this year, with the exception of
a bad one of our homicide rate, which is up.
But last year's homicide rate was the lowest since 1954.
We're still short police officers,
but we have said rebuilding the ranks,
rebuilding the ranks of our police officers
is a huge priority of ours.
10 days ago, I went to a
graduating class of the academy.
We had 41 people graduate.
It's the largest graduating class since 2017.
We're expecting—last year we had 5,000 people
apply to be police officers.
This year we're on pace for 10,000 people to apply
to be, or to be police officers, or apply to be.
So people want to be.
Police officers again in San Francisco.
And the vast majority of San Franciscans believe in
those common sense solutions and policies,
and it's working.
[HOST] What have been the easiest or hardest?
What's been surprisingly easy or hard about making this happen?
I'm sure there's things you came in and you thought, oh,
this is going to be intractable.
And something that you came in and it's like,
oh, this is much more complicated than I expected.
[DANIEL LURIE] I think I've never had somebody ask me
about easy in this job.
Usually people ask me what the hardest part is.
But I think-
I think what we tried to come in with a new approach,
and that was to collaborate.
To collaborate across our departments, to collaborate
across the supervisors.
I mean, this, it's a notorious thing that the mayor and the 11
supervisors, our city council,
like, are supposed to not get along.
And I, in my first few weeks in office,
I went around to every supervisor's office.
I would just walk down the hall.
We're all in the same hall.
They're on one side of the building, I'm on the other.
And I'd say, "Hey..."
"How are you?"
And people were like, "Wait, what are you doing over here?"
"You shouldn't be over on this side of the building."
And I've continued that.
I walked into a supervisor's office yesterday before I
went to question time at the Board of Supervisors
and handed a supervisor a birthday gift.
And like we're trying to build that
collaborative spirit.
We have department head meetings once a week,
our large agency on Tuesday mornings at 9:00 AM.
The top 20 departments, we all gather at one
conference room table
and we share out what's going on.
That was not happening at City Hall for—
A long time.
And so you're all at the business school, like this,
this just is common sense.
This isn't...
I didn't make stuff up, but we've brought this in-house.
And then what I'd say about, you know,
on the public safety front or the police front,
like if I see a police officer on the street.
I shake their hand.
If I see a firefighter on the street, I shake their
hand, I say, "Thank you."
Like little things, I believe, go a long way.
And so I don't know if that's easy, but it's common sense,
it's simple, and it takes a lot of effort and work to do it.
Or not effort, but you have to
keep doing it and really build that
sense of we're all in this together.
And I can't tell you, I've gone to every police
academy graduation.
I went to the firefighters' graduation.
I try to do that for the sheriffs and just show
that we're there to...
We need them.
I need them.
The city needs them.
And so.
[HOST] So building on this question of, like, building connections with
different groups and different constituencies, a lot of the
things that a city needs are just intensely political issues,
like things about housing, transportation, land use.
You're like, "You don't need to tell me."
Right. So these are very intensely political questions.
And there are also things on which-
Cities tend to have a lot of interest group activity,
like very intensely engaged groups of citizens or people
who have different states in it, very different views.
And San Francisco is especially famous for being, as we would
say in political science, an interest group-rich environment.
[DANIEL LURIE] Yes, yes.
[HOST] And so this means you have the challenge and opportunity
to work with lots of different groups, some of whom you
agree with, and some of whom disagree with you.
And what have you learned sort of over the time about how to
effectively work with all these different groups, whether it's
business, nonprofits, unions, local community groups?
How do you think about that structure
of interest group activity?
[DANIEL LURIE] Everybody does have an opinion in San Francisco.
You are correct.
I haven't thought...
Well, I haven't thought about it that much.
Although all I will say is,
so we have an incredibly
difficult budget that we have to...
I present a budget on June 1st.
And if we do nothing, we will have in four or five
years, we will have a billion-plus budget deficit.
We have reined in spending in our city
over the last 15 months.
We're going to continue to lean into that.
And I started talking to people in October and
November of last year about...
The budget problems that we have this year.
And we have groups coming in from all over.
Every interest group that you can imagine has come and sat in
room 201 across from my office.
And I've said to them for seven months
the same thing that I say to
The API community to the LGBTQ plus community
to the trans community.
We have a budget crisis,
and I so appreciate everything that you all are doing,
but we all are going to have to take some of the pain.
And I think the most important thing is
that you say the same thing to everyone.
You don't cater to this one group and say one thing,
and then you walk into another room and you say something else.
And I've said this about our public safety officials:
We have to take pain there, too.
And so I think being honest.
I walked into office in a very different manner
than most electeds.
First, I had never been in elected office.
And really, very few people
of those interest groups supported me.
No one thought I could win.
And so I came in with a lot less baggage.
And I don't care about what's next.
I don't have political aspirations beyond this job.
And people might not believe me.
That's okay. You don't have to.
But I don't.
I really want to fix the city that I was born and raised in.
I wanna fix the city that I'm raising my two young kids in.
My wife and I are...
And when you just have that focus in mind,
I think you can be honest, and you can be straight,
and you can take
the daggers that are coming your way.
And do what's right for the city, and that's my focus.
[HOST] So you said you mentioned coming
into office and not having had
elected office experience, but you had experience
leading Tipping Point.
[DANIEL LURIE] Yes.
[HOST] And so I'm curious what you learned from that
experience leading, starting, and then
leading that organization for quite a while, and what
of that carried over into, you know, being mayor?
[DANIEL LURIE] Well, I mean, it's the people in this room,
you all get this.
It's, it, it, you—
You definitely don't want to just rely on City
Hall to get things done.
That would not have been smart.
You can't just rely on philanthropy to get things
done, and you can't just rely on the business sector.
Like, they all need to work together.
I think we're seeing that in real
time with the Partnership for San Francisco growing up over
the last year in San Francisco.
We have a downtown development corporation that is
growing up to help us.
Really go after the Union Square and the financial district
and get retailers and get businesses back downtown.
And I know you'll be talking about that later today.
So we need each other.
And at Tipping Point, we always looked at
ourselves as the seed capital, the risk capital.
Let's take shots on new approaches to solving
issues of poverty.
And then if it worked, then we'd say, "Hey," to
mayors across the region, whether it was
Mayor Liccardo or Mayor Lee
or the Oakland mayor, we would say-
Here, this works.
You should take it.
The money is at the government level.
And we always were partnering with both the
government and the business.
And now, as mayor, I want to engage those,
I want to engage all of you, and I want to engage the
nonprofit sector because we
can't do it alone at City Hall.
[HOST] How do you approach those regional and—
Because, I mean, many of the issues
that a city faces, San Francisco's what,
one-eighth of the Bay Area's population,
something like that? Depends on
what you define the Bay Area as.
[DANIEL LURIE] Right, right.
[HOST] But it's, I mean, it's this huge deal
economically, symbolically, you know, culturally.
It's a famous, famous city.
But it's not even the biggest city in the Bay
Area, actually, right?
That's San Jose.
[DANIEL LURIE] But it's the best.
Yeah. Let's be clear.
Sorry. Sorry. Yeah.
Sorry to my friends everywhere else.
Okay.
And I will also say, with the moment we're living in,
you all know this better than I do, AI that.
Tech ecosystem.
It's San Francisco now.
It's not, sorry, it's not down here.
Every venture firm has an office in San Francisco, has to.
These companies are kind of recentering themselves on
San Francisco, and it's an exciting time to be in the city.
I want to be very clear though, because I know I'm in a
business-friendly environment.
I was on stage at an AI conference the other day and
It was funny, someone said I was pivoting when I said this.
There's no pivot here.
The most important industry to San Francisco has been,
is today, and will be in the future, is tourism.
And we love that we're the home of AI.
We wanna lean into that.
But I just wanna be clear, I say it everywhere,
Tourism is our number one thing,
which is why the public safety is so important.
It's why we have to get people off the street
and into recovery beds.
It's why we are...
My third priority that I always talk about is making us a,
a business-friendly city again around permitting,
around small businesses and restaurants, and we
have the best restaurants.
In the world, not just in
the country, in the world or
in San Francisco.
And how do we make life easier for small
business, medium business, and big business?
We want all of that in San Francisco.
We want that revenue, that tax revenue
in San Francisco, and I think those are the
three things that apply to tourism,
that apply to
Technology and businesses
wanting to come back to San Francisco.
[HOST] Given, and actually, tourism is something
I wanted to talk about specifically
because I think it's interesting because
people get a lot of information from around the country and
around the world about San Francisco in a lot of ways.
I mean, you could think in some sense,
you know, a fair number of
people get, you know, a few ads a day,
negative about San Francisco in their
news channels.
You know, it's like this problem in San Francisco,
that just kind of like... How do you go about telling the
story about what's going on in San Francisco and sharing,
changing the narrative?
[DANIEL LURIE] Yep.
[HOST] Nationally, and is it different internationally?
Or do you see it—
[DANIEL LURIE] No, I think—
[HOST] is there distinctions,
or how do you think about that problem?
[DANIEL LURIE] So people, you know, I think, uh—
Back to one of your earlier questions, what was easiest,
what was challenging?
I think our biggest challenge, and I think we did this well
in our first year in office, was changing the narrative
about our city.
We were punched for three or four years.
And it's why I ran for office, because a lot of
those criticisms were true.
I could not explain to my two kids,
why they were seeing what they were seeing on the streets,
and none of us could, and we had become numb to it.
But now, I really
fundamentally believe that we're getting better.
Coverage nationally and internationally.
People are hearing, "Oh, San Francisco's on the rise."
And it's because it's true.
It's because of our restaurants and our arts
and our culture and AI and tech.
And hopefully, it's because we have
a board of supervisors and a mayor that's not
looking to just be at war with each other all the time,
but to fix the problems that we all know are real.
And so I think...
I, I, I don't know.
I think what I'm hearing,
and I hope you all are
hearing when you're traveling.
By the way, this felt like a
foreign trip for me to come
all the way down here.
I really don't ever leave the city.
I'm doing my first international
trip actually to Shanghai and Seoul
next week to visit our
two important sister cities.
I want to bring tours, you know,
I want to sell San Francisco
in those two amazing cities.
I want tourism coming back
from those countries.
So I think.
We're addressing the narrative,
I think is much more positive now.
Mm-hmm.
And what I would say is we had to start with ourselves.
Two years ago, San Franciscans,
22% of San Franciscans thought we were on the right track.
I've seen,
someone told me about a poll
that was done just about five days ago,
and it had 70% of San Franciscans
thought we were on the right track.
I mean, well, I don't think
there's a city in the country that has a
70% right-track number on it besides-
[HOST] Yeah, political polling in general-
Yeah, it's just not a common thing.
[DANIEL LURIE] Yes, right.
[HOST] Yeah. Right.
[DANIEL LURIE] So that's, that's a...
So it's, it's working.
[HOST] Yeah.
[DANIEL LURIE] But every day we gotta win.
Yeah, every day we gotta win that battle.
And frankly, I am far from satisfied.
I told you about my experience this morning.
Last night I was heading home late—
or two nights ago—from the Bruce Springsteen concert.
That was fun.
I brought my 12-year-old to that, by the way.
He was like, "It took him a little bit to get into it,"
but it's okay.
He appreciated it.
I will say this:
I didn't like what I saw on some of our streets.
[HOST] Yeah, yeah.
[DANIEL LURIE] So I want everybody to know that we're doing better,
but we have so much work to do.
[HOST] That's interesting.
How much, what role do you see events playing in this?
I mean, I remember seeing stories during the recent
Super Bowl, like tourists like, "I went to San Francisco
and I was shocked."
"Yeah, it wasn't a hellhole," or something.
That was kind of the reaction.
Or, you know, or the upcoming World Cup
or, you know, conferences.
[DANIEL LURIE] Is this... That was... that's a great thing,
thank you for bringing that up because-
Yeah, you know, we had Media Row, or now
I don't remember the new title is because there's no...
It used to be called Radio Row.
That's not a thing anymore.
But we had, I think, 12,000 credentialed media.
In town.
And the vast majority
was positive.
And we had people from
the middle of the country saying,
"I love your city,
it's so beautiful."
And so that was a huge win for us.
And then we're gonna always have
our haters that just simply-
See San Francisco and reflectively say,
"Oh, that's terrible."
"That place is terrible, because of values or whatever it is."
So we can't really worry about them.
But so that helped us really turn the tide.
[HOST] I want to turn in a different direction.
So you mentioned AI earlier, and obviously it is true.
I mean, huge flourishing of innovation
in AI in San Francisco.
And how do you think about making sure that the city
is the place going forward?
Yeah, where...
I mean, you think about cities in the world that
have these innovative, just innovative industry
after innovative industry, or waves of changes coming through,
and there's some cities that seem to do this
well, some cities that seem to do that less well.
And San Francisco's done this multiple times.
[DANIEL LURIE] Yeah. Over, and we keep doing it.
[HOST] Yeah. What do you think is the core of that,
and how do you set up the city for continued success doing that
with, like, the next big thing?
[DANIEL LURIE] I mean, I, I know AI's
a really big thing now, but...
Well, I can go right to—I mean, I have one answer,
which is, you know, what we've been really focused on
around making sure that we create enough housing,
enough educational opportunities, childcare,
and making sure that not only are we supporting
the AI industry, but everything that comes out of that:
our restaurants, our arts,
our cultural institutions.
Like, I believe firmly that our creative class is
what has always driven San Francisco forward.
And out of that comes these innovative ideas,
whether it was the computer or the internet or now AI.
Like, it happens because of a really...
Great ecosystem.
And it's not just about tech employees.
It's about all of our great cultural institutions.
And for those to run, you need to make sure
people can be housed,
that they can go to great public schools.
We are the first country, first city in the country.
To provide opportunity and access to free
early childhood care.
There's other— I've got some friends
on the East Coast that are claiming that
they're going after it.
We've already done it in San Francisco.
If you were a family of four
making $230,000 a year or less,
you qualify or you have the opportunity to get
free early childhood.
It can save people up to $36,000 a year.
If you're a family of four making $310,000 dollars,
and we started that in January, if you're making
$310,000 dollars a year or less,
you qualify for 50% off of that.
And so you create that dynamic in our city.
We keep young families, we keep those creatives
staying in San Francisco.
Like, that helps drive our city forward.
I had the honor of meeting
Francis Ford Coppola yesterday.
And he came in, he asked me a question.
He goes, "Do you know
who Jane Jacobs is?"
And I was like, "Yep."
My wife is, you know, when I met my wife in
New York City, like, we started talking about Jane
Jacobs and Eyes on the Street,
and just how you need
this dynamism on the streets.
And then Francis started talking about our
neighborhoods, like North Beach.
I mean, Jackson Square's up and coming,
like the Mission District.
Ocean Beach, by the way,
right now, out in the Sunset is
Thriving.
Our Sunset at Ninth and Irving is incredible.
[HOST] Yeah, yeah.
[DANIEL LURIE] Like, we have these neighborhoods.
It's a great neighborhood.
And those neighborhoods create that energy that we need,
so we have to make sure our neighborhoods are thriving.
Once again, this is where I'm now,
I'm learning how to be a politician.
Safety, clean streets, getting people to housing
and off the street and the recovery.
Like those neighborhoods
always say, "Hey, there's still too many
people suffering on my streets."
"I need more police officers walking the beat."
So my job at City Hall, I fundamentally believe,
is to do the basics,
to allow our neighborhoods to thrive,
and then you all and the business community
and our entrepreneurs and our creatives,
Yeah, they help our city continue to
Dominate in terms of what's next and what's on the
cutting edge for the world.
[HOST] But there's a potential irony here in that when
you have flourishing business success and all sorts of new
things being developed, and frankly lots of people
getting rich doing these things,
that often puts a lot of strain
on particularly housing supply.
Like I remember when I was living in the city in the '90s,
I can't remember which one of the local papers was,
it had like a cartoon.
It was like Stanford, the first completely
gentrified city.
And so the concern is that if you have these
economic developments, it's great for a set of people,
but it also can make the city not work for people who can
no longer afford there.
And this has been a repeated
concern over the decades.
Whenever there's a boom in San Francisco,
there's people who are longtime residents or
the children of longtime residents and who are like,
"We can't afford to live in the city that we know and love."
[DANIEL LURIE] Yeah.
[HOST] How do we keep the character of the city the same
while having...
But you need the economic success at the same time,
and how do you think about that as mayor?
[DANIEL LURIE] First off, I don't think we
should ever try to be the same
or aspire to be the same.
We're evolving.
We're a dynamic city.
We're changing.
We need to continue to grow.
And you're right,
this affordability issue
has been an issue
for decades and decades
and generations and generations.
And this is where it's
really frustrating to say
that we're progressive.
We're not.
In many ways, we are not progressive
because we don't allow housing to get built.
And so we spent a lot of time
in our first year in office focused on
a rezoning.
Rezoning the west side and the north side to
create more housing.
And we weren't going crazy.
We were trying to do it our way and not the Sacramento way.
Sacramento was imposing this on all the counties in the state.
But we were going from four stories on the west
side to along our commercial corridors
and near transit hubs, going up to six stories.
Mm-hmm.
Six.
And it was, like, met with just this,
"Don't change my neighborhood."
But-
We're gonna create more affordable neighborhoods.
We're gonna actually create more customers for our small
businesses if we go to six or eight stories along
Irving or Judah or Clement.
And by the way, this will take decades to see in action.
And I'm telling you, I think we hit the sweet spot,
because right now we are being sued by the YIMBYs
for not going far enough.
And the NIMBYs are also suing us.
So we're getting it from both sides.
So I think we hit the middle.
So we need to build more housing.
There's no question about that.
[HOST] I mean, it's always struck me.
When I lived in the city, so I was in there in the mid-'90s,
and then I moved, I got a job in Chicago, moved to Chicago,
lived in Lakeview.
And, you know, Chicago housing prices were vastly
cheaper than San Francisco housing prices.
And I also noticed the entire street north of me in Chicago,
it was Briar, um, between Broadway and Belmont, no,
Broadway and Clark in Chicago.
It was all these old single-family homes.
They were kind of decrepit.
They were kind of worn down.
And within the three years that I, and later my wife and I,
lived in an apartment there, um-
Almost all of those were bought, torn down, and three
flats were put in there.
They tripled the housing density in this awesome
neighborhood in Chicago.
[DANIEL LURIE] Uh-huh.
[HOST] And I was thinking, I was like, "That was inconceivable in the
San Francisco that I lived in."
[DANIEL LURIE] Yeah.
[HOST] And so, how do you think about just the mechanics
of getting housing built?
In the city.
And I'm sure you've thought about this a lot.
Like, how do you—you know,
what makes it possible to actually do it
Well, as opposed to in principle?
[DANIEL LURIE] First, it's zoning.
So, doing that is helpful.
We've seen a lot of development down in Mission Bay.
[HOST] Yeah, and Mission Rock.
[DANIEL LURIE] Yes, around Chase Center and around the baseball stadium.
And it was actually, there was an article
in the San Francisco Chronicle.
By this incredible writer who talked about how it felt
like Parisian, like this new neighborhood down there.
Yeah. I don't know if people agree with that, but...
[HOST] No, but my 17-year-old daughter
goes up and hangs out there.
[DANIEL LURIE] Yeah, it's beautiful.
[HOST] She takes the Caltrain up there
to hang out in that neighborhood.
[DANIEL LURIE] And there's lots of restaurants,
and there's art galleries,
and we obviously have these great stadiums.
And there's great food.
So...
I think about it as, once again,
our job at City Hall is the zoning.
We have these macroeconomic
factors, the cost of—
construction, the cost of labor—
the cost of all of that.
So, like, I can't.
One thing that I always—
I hope everybody takes away from this,
also, I want to tell you this is that I can only control
so much and electeds can only do so much.
And to remember that and not to try to do everything
or say you're going to do.
